implementation_notes: Scala runs on the JVM, so the zero-dependency realization is java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue: producers put items (from any thread, a Future executor or an actor), and a fixed pool of consumer threads loops on take(); ArrayBlockingQueue is the bounded form, offer/poll with a timeout give bounded waits, and shutdown uses poison pills or interrupts. Futures alone are not a queue - when the hand-off must be a real bounded buffer, pair the queue with an executor, or let a ThreadPoolExecutor backed by an ArrayBlockingQueue be the buffer. Blocking take() occupies a pool thread, so the pool size is the real concurrency budget.
code_sketch:
import java.util.concurrent._

val queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue[Job](1024)
val consumers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)
(0 until 4).foreach(_ => consumers.execute(() =>
  while (true) handle(queue.take())))
queue.put(job)                          // blocks while full
pitfalls: take()/put() throw InterruptedException; Scala code must either propagate it or catch it, restore the interrupt flag and exit the loop.
new LinkedBlockingQueue() (no capacity) is the usual JVM shortcut that turns decoupling into unbounded memory growth.
Blocking take() inside a scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext can starve unrelated tasks when the pool is saturated with blocked consumers.
Mixing poison-pill shutdown with interrupt-based shutdown leaves consumers in an unknown state; pick one protocol and implement it consistently.

variants.name: cats-effect Queue (purely functional)
variants.idiom_name: cats.effect.std.Queue[F, A] with offer/take and an explicit capacity policy
variants.implementation_notes: cats-effect's Queue[F, A] is the purely functional realization: Queue.bounded[IO, A](capacity) makes offer fiber-blocking while full and take fiber-blocking while empty, and the constructor family states the policy up front - synchronous (= bounded(0), a rendezvous), unbounded, dropping(capacity) and circularBuffer(capacity) - which turns the full-queue decision into an explicit construction. Fiber blocking suspends the fiber without occupying a platform thread, so many consumers are cheap, and the queue is split into QueueSource (Functor) and QueueSink (Contravariant) so each side can depend on only the half it uses.
pitfalls: Choosing unbounded or synchronous by accident changes the semantics: synchronous has no buffer at all, unbounded removes backpressure.
Blocking JDK calls inside an IO must be wrapped in IO.blocking (not plain IO), or the compute pool starves while fibers wait.
Consumer fiber errors kill only that fiber while the queue keeps being consumed by the survivors - deliberate, but silent work loss if it is not monitored.
